title: Men enjoy five hours more leisure time per week than women
meta_description: Men in the UK enjoy nearly five more hours of leisure time per week than women, ONS analysis reveals.

Men enjoy five hours more leisure time per week than women

lede: Men in the UK enjoy nearly five more hours of leisure time per week than women, ONS analysis reveals.

body.text: 9 January 2018
Men in the UK enjoy nearly five more hours of leisure time per week than women, ONS analysis reveals.
In 2015, men took, on average, 43 hours of leisure time per week, whereas women took around 38 hours of leisure time.

When considering the amount of leisure men and women took 15 years earlier, it suggests that there is a growth in inequality between men and women when it comes to taking leisure time. Men are now taking quite a lot more time each week for leisure and women are taking less compared with 2000.

body.h4: Leisure hours taken per week, by sex, 2000 and 2015
body.text: Leisure time for women could be less than for men because although women are more frequently engaged in part-time work than men, they spend more time completing unpaid work such as household chores and childcare. The hours spent on unpaid work are likely to replace those hours that could have been spent on leisure activities.

body.h3: People living with children take less leisure time than those living alone
body.text: People living with children take less leisure time than those living alone

body.h3: People living with children take less leisure time than those living alone
body.text: People living in households with a child under the age of 15 years report taking up to 14 hours per week less leisure time than those living on their own.

body.h3: People living with children take less leisure time than those living alone
body.text: People living in households with children reported spending less of their leisure time resting, particularly those from single parent households. Those from households without children, however, spent more time doing things like watching television and reading. Though people living with children also spent the majority of their leisure time consuming mass media, they did so for less time.

body.h3: People living with children take less leisure time than those living alone
body.text: Men consistently took more leisure time than women regardless of how old the child in their household was.

body.h3: Parents whose youngest child was aged five to ten took more leisure time in 2015 than in 2000
body.text: Focusing specifically on parents who live with their children, those whose youngest child was aged between five and ten years old are now taking more leisure time than they did in 2000. Mothers took an hour and a half more time and fathers took two hours more.

body.h3: Parents whose youngest child was aged five to ten took more leisure time in 2015 than in 2000
body.text: The amount of leisure time a parent took increased with the age of a child in both 2000 and 2015. The only decrease seen was for those parents whose youngest child was under five.

body.h4: Notes
body.text: Leisure time in this analysis includes a range of activities including: socialising, cultural activities, resting and taking time out, sports or outdoor pursuits, hobbies, computing and games, mass media, eating out and travel associated with these leisure activities. The survey recorded the main activity that a person was completing at the time. It excludes paid work, unpaid work such as chores or childcare, study, travel unrelated to leisure activities, and actions necessary for existing such as eating and sleeping.

body.h3: The older people get, the more leisure time they take
body.h4: Notes
body.text: The survey includes those aged eight and over in the UK.
